title: The $n$-torsion of an abelian variety is etale
statement:
Let $A$ be an abelian variety
of dimension $g$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ and let
$n$ be prime to $\operatorname{char}k$. Then
$A[n]=\ker([n])$ ([def-sc-mult-n]) is a finite etale
group scheme over $k$, the
canonical base change map

$$
A[n](k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }A[n](k')
$$

is an isomorphism for every extension $k\subseteq k'$ of
algebraically closed fields, and

$$
A[n](k)\cong(\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z)^{2g}.
$$

proof.text: For n prime to the characteristic, [lem-sc-mult-n-finite-flat] gives that A[n] is finite flat of order n^{2g}, and [lem-sc-mult-n-etale-kernel] gives that it is etale. Applying [lem-sc-finite-etale-points] to A[n] gives |A[n](k)| = n^{2g} and identifies the canonical map A[n](k) \to A[n](k') as a bijection. Thus A[n] is a finite etale group scheme and the asserted base-change map is an isomorphism of groups.

The surjectivity statement [lem-sc-isogeny-surjective] for every positive integer implies that A(k) is divisible, and [lem-sc-av-commutative] makes it an abelian group. For each prime power ell^e dividing n, the equality A(k)[ell^e] = A[ell^e](k) follows from the definition of the kernel, while, since ell divides n and so ell^e is prime to char k, [lem-sc-mult-n-finite-flat] gives that A[ell^e] is finite flat of order ell^(2ge), [lem-sc-mult-n-etale-kernel] gives that it is etale, and [lem-sc-finite-etale-points] then gives this subgroup order ell^(2ge). In particular its ell-torsion has order ell^(2g), so [lem-sc-divisible-group-structure] gives A[ell^e](k) isomorphic to (Z/ell^e Z)^(2g).

Write n as the product of its pairwise coprime prime powers. The coprime torsion decomposition [lem-sc-coprime-torsion-decomposition], applied to the Z-module A[n](k), identifies A[n](k) with the product of the prime-power subgroups. The Chinese remainder isomorphism identifies the product of the groups (Z/ell_i^e_i Z)^(2g) with (Z/n Z)^(2g). The kernel definition identifies these point subgroups with the corresponding A[ell_i^e_i](k), so this is the claimed group isomorphism.

blueprint_update.statement:
Let $A$ be an abelian variety
of dimension $g$ over a field $k$ and let
$n\geq1$ be prime to $\operatorname{char}k$. Then
$A[n]=\ker([n])$ ([def-sc-mult-n]) is a finite etale
group scheme over $k$. If moreover $k$ is algebraically closed, the
canonical base change map

$$
A[n](k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }A[n](k')
$$

is a bijection for every extension $k\subseteq k'$ of
algebraically closed fields, and the $n$-torsion subgroup of $A(k)$
satisfies

$$
A[n](k)=A(k)[n]\cong(\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z)^{2g}.
$$

proof.text:
By [lem-sc-isogeny-facts](b), $A[n]$ is a finite flat group
scheme of order $n^{2g}$ over the field $k$, and $n^{2g}$ is prime to
$\operatorname{char}k$ ([lem-sc-mult-n-finite-flat]); by
[lem-sc-fg-order-prime-etale], which holds over any field, it is
etale (equivalently, $[n]$ is etale, by [lem-sc-mult-n-etale-kernel]).

Now let $k$ be algebraically closed. By [lem-sc-finite-etale-points]
the map $A[n](k)\to A[n](k')$ is a bijection. It remains to identify
the group structure. Since $[n]$ is surjective on $k$-points for
every $n$ ([lem-sc-isogeny-surjective]), the group $A(k)$
is divisible; by [lem-sc-av-commutative] it is abelian. For a
prime power $\ell^e$ with $\ell\neq\operatorname{char}k$, the
subgroup $A(k)[\ell^e]=A[\ell^e](k)$ has order
$\ell^{2ge}$ ([lem-sc-finite-etale-points] applied to
$A[\ell^e]$, of order $\ell^{2ge}$ by
[lem-sc-isogeny-facts](b)), so the divisible group $A(k)$
satisfies $|A(k)[\ell]|=\ell^{2g}$, and by
[lem-sc-divisible-group-structure]

$$
A[\ell^e](k)\cong(\mathbf Z/\ell^e\mathbf Z)^{2g}.
$$

For general $n=\prod_i\ell_i^{e_i}$ prime to
$\operatorname{char}k$, the closed subgroup schemes
$A[\ell_i^{e_i}]$ have coprime orders, so
$A[n]=A[\ell_1^{e_1}]\times\cdots\times A[\ell_r^{e_r}]$ as group
schemes (by Bezout's identity the multiplication maps give the
direct product decomposition), and

$$
A[n](k)\cong\prod_i(\mathbf Z/\ell_i^{e_i}\mathbf Z)^{2g}
\cong(\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z)^{2g}
$$

by the Chinese remainder theorem.
